summary: Defines how the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) produces, reviews, and publishes its own documents as RFCs. The IAB occasionally issues statements and architectural guidance, and this memo sets out the process those documents follow on their way into the RFC Series.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4845 explains how the Internet Architecture Board prepares, reviews, and publishes its documents as RFCs. For an Informational RFC, the process includes an IETF-wide call for comment before the document goes to the RFC Editor.

questions: how does the iab publish rfcs
what is the iab call for comment
subtitle: The review and publication process for documents that the IAB publishes as RFCs.

tldr.problem: The IAB publishes statements, activity reports, and other documents as RFCs, so it needs a process for reviewing and approving those documents.
tldr.mechanism: For Informational documents, the IAB publishes a draft, requests comments across the IETF, considers feedback, and sends a ready document to the RFC Editor.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4845 describes the IAB publication process. It says the Call for Comment period is normally no shorter than four weeks.

facts.label: Call for Comment period
facts.value: Normally no shorter than four weeks

today: RFC 4845 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. It describes the process for publishing IAB documents.

sections.title: Which Documents the IAB Publishes
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) publishes RFCs that record its consideration of an issue, report on IAB activities such as workshops, or share documents that the IAB believes would benefit the IETF community even though they did not come from an IETF Working Group.

The RFC says most IAB documents are Informational. The IAB generally does not publish Standards-Track or Experimental RFCs. If it publishes a document as a Best Current Practice, that document follows the IETF standards-stream approval process.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB publishes its own statements, reports on its activities, and other documents it thinks will help the IETF community. Most are Informational RFCs.

sections.title: Review and Approval by the IAB
sections.content:
For a document that records an IAB statement or position, the IAB discusses and refines the text internally. It approves publication only when its members agree on the document's main substance.

For some documents, the IAB does not take responsibility for technical correctness. For example, approving a workshop report means the IAB considers it a faithful report of the workshop and believes the subject matters to the community. The document's introduction should make the IAB's role clear, and it may note significant IAB concerns about an item.
sections.plainLanguage: When the IAB publishes its position, it approves the main content. For a workshop report, approval may mean only that the report is faithful and the subject is relevant.

sections.title: The Publication Process
sections.content:
The IAB first decides that a document is an IAB document. It then publishes an IAB draft, named with the pattern draft-iab-*, reviews comments, and may seek input from specific people or groups. Documents intended as Best Current Practices go to the IESG with a sponsoring Area Director and follow the process described for that stream.

For an Informational RFC, the IAB chair issues an IETF-wide Call for Comment on the IETF Announce mailing list. The comment period is normally no shorter than four weeks. The IAB considers the comments and decides whether to publish or revise the document and seek more input. A ready document goes to the RFC Editor for publication.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB publishes a draft and asks the IETF community for comments. It considers the feedback, makes any needed revisions, and sends the finished Informational document to the RFC Editor.
